lead: Numerical control (NC) means running a machine tool from numbers instead of from cams, stops and a skilled hand on the feed wheel. The numbers sit in a part program, and each line of that program is a block. In the first NC machines the program lived on punched tape; a reader fed it to a machine control unit, which pulsed the axis motors. CNC moved the program into a computer inside the machine. DNC moved the program store out to a central computer that serves many machines. This chapter follows that move and what each step bought the shop floor.
prereq: You need: Unit 5 for the slideways, leadscrew and axis motions of a lathe or a milling machine; the block format of a part program itself is in 6.4.

sections.h3: Punched tape and the machine control unit

blocks.text: On a centre lathe, cams, stops and change gears fix the sequence of cuts. Change the part, and you change the hardware. NC replaced that hardware with a program: a list of blocks, each block saying where the tool goes, how fast, and with what spindle speed.

The classic NC chain has four parts. The tape reader reads the punched tape one block at a time. The machine control unit (MCU) decodes the block. The axis drives turn the decoded numbers into motion of the slides. A feedback device, if one is fitted, reports the slide position back to the MCU.

items: The reader pulls one block of characters off the tape.
The MCU decodes the block: axis words, feed word, spindle word.
The MCU generates pulses at a rate set by the feed word.
Each pulse drives the axis motor, and the leadscrew moves the slide by one basic length unit (BLU).
The MCU reads the next block and repeats.

blocks.where: v is the slide feed in mm/s, f<sub>p</sub> is the pulse frequency in pulses per second, and BLU is the basic length unit in mm per pulse. Multiply v by 60 to get mm/min.

blocks.text: Early MCUs were hard-wired. The logic was a fixed circuit, so a canned cycle or a new interpolation scheme needed new boards. The tape itself was weak: it tore, it stretched in a hot shop, and one bad character stopped the job. To run the same part again you rewound the tape.
The reader is fast and the cutter is slow. A reader can hand over a block in a fraction of a second and then sit idle while the tool cuts. That idle time is the subject of the worked example.

sections.h3: What CNC adds on top of NC

blocks.text: CNC puts a computer inside the machine control unit. The part program is typed in or transferred once and stored in memory. The machine then runs from memory, and the tape reader disappears from the chain.

items: Editing at the machine: correct one feed value without punching a new tape.
Canned cycles: one block drills a whole row of holes with pecking, instead of a long list of blocks.
Tool length and cutter radius compensation: the programmer writes the part outline, and the real tool size is entered at the machine.
Diagnostics: the controller reports a failed board or a loose encoder instead of leaving you with a dead machine.
Graphics: the controller draws the tool path before the first cut.
Subprograms, macros and background editing: write the next job while the present one runs.

blocks.text: All six are software features. In hard-wired NC each one had to be built in hardware, so a control offered only the few features its boards were wired for, and any new one meant new boards. The heart of CNC is therefore not the computer itself but the stored program and the soft-wired logic that can be changed without a soldering iron. The controller side of this, including interpolation, is in 6.3.
A computer can also hold a file and talk to another computer. That is the door through which DNC walked in.
DNC carries two meanings and they are often mixed. Always say which one you mean.

items: Direct numerical control (older meaning): one central computer holds the programs and drives a group of machines, usually with no tape reader on each machine.

Distributed numerical control (newer meaning): each machine keeps its own CNC controller, and a central server distributes part programs, collects production counts and tracks tool life over a shop network.

blocks.text: The older direct link was built in three ways.

items: Behind the tape reader (BTR): the computer feeds characters into the existing reader port, so the old MCU never knows the tape is gone. Cheapest, and it keeps the old machine.
Behind the MCU: the computer sends motion commands straight to the axis drives and the MCU becomes a slave. More capable, but tied to one maker's hardware.
Special machine control: the MCU is replaced outright by the central computer. Full control, and full dependence on that computer.

blocks.text: All three share one weakness: a computer failure stops the whole group. Distributed DNC fixes that. Each machine can run from its own memory, and the server is only a library.

examples.question: An NC part program has 4,200 characters in 70 blocks. The tape reader reads 300 characters per second. Each block takes 25 s of machining time. Find (a) the characters per block, (b) the reading time per block, (c) the time the reader is idle per block, and (d) the percentage of the cycle for which the reader is idle.
steps: Characters per block = total characters ÷ number of blocks = 4,200 ÷ 70 = 60 characters per block.
Reading time per block = characters per block ÷ reader speed = 60 ÷ 300 = 0.2 s.
Machining time per block = 25 s is the time the tool cuts. So the total cycle is reading plus machining = 0.2 + 25 = 25.2 s, and the idle time is 25 − 0.2 = 24.8 s.
Idle percentage is measured against the whole cycle, reading plus machining: idle time ÷ total cycle time × 100 = 24.8 ÷ 25.2 × 100 = 98.4 %.
examples.answer: The reader needs 0.2 s per block and is idle 24.8 s of every 25.2 s cycle, that is 98.4 % idle.
examples.check:
chars = 4200
blocks = 70
rate = 300
cut = 25
cpb = chars / blocks
t_read = cpb / rate
cycle = cut + t_read
idle = cut - t_read
pct = idle / cycle * 100
print(round(cpb, 4))
print(round(t_read, 4))
print(round(cycle, 4))
print(round(idle, 4))
print(round(pct, 1))

traps: CNC is not simply 'NC plus a computer'. The examinable difference is the stored program in memory plus soft-wired logic; editing, compensation, canned cycles and diagnostics all follow from that.
DNC is not a control loop. DNC says where the program lives; open loop and closed loop say whether the slide is measured. See 6.3.
DNC has two meanings. Direct numerical control is one computer driving many MCUs; distributed numerical control is a server handing files to independent CNCs. Say which one you mean.
Unit slip: BLU is mm per pulse and pulse frequency is pulses per second, so v = f<sub>p</sub> × BLU comes out in mm/s. Multiply by 60 for mm/min.
A reader that is idle for almost the whole cycle is not a slow reader. It is a fast reader waiting for a slow cutter, and that is why the tool, not the tape, set the pace of an NC shop.

quiz.q: Name the four parts of the classic NC chain, from tape to slide.
quiz.a: Tape reader, machine control unit (MCU), axis drives and the feedback device that reports slide position. On a simple open-loop machine the leadscrew and slide replace the feedback device.

quiz.q: Why was hard-wired logic a limitation in NC?
quiz.a: The control function was fixed by the circuit. Adding a canned cycle or a new interpolation scheme meant new boards and a rewired controller, so the machine could not be upgraded in the field and every feature cost hardware.

quiz.q: A tape holds 3,000 characters in 60 blocks. The reader runs at 250 characters per second and each block needs 20 s of machining. Find the reading time per block and the percentage of the cycle the reader is idle.
quiz.a: Characters per block = 3,000 ÷ 60 = 50. Reading time = 50 ÷ 250 = 0.2 s. Total cycle = 20 + 0.2 = 20.2 s. Idle time = 20 − 0.2 = 19.8 s. Idle percentage = idle time ÷ total cycle time × 100 = 19.8 ÷ 20.2 × 100 = 98.0 %.

quiz.q: Distinguish direct numerical control from distributed numerical control.
quiz.a: Direct: one central computer supplies motion or character data to many machines, which may have no program store of their own. Distributed: each machine has its own CNC controller and memory, and a server only distributes files and collects data.

quiz.q: List the three ways a DNC computer can be linked to an older machine.
quiz.a: Behind the tape reader (BTR), behind the MCU (drives fed directly with the MCU as slave), and special machine control where the MCU is replaced by the central computer.

quiz.q: A shop has 12 CNC machines and no central program store. Give two reasons to add a distributed DNC server and one risk it brings.
quiz.a: Reasons: programs are stored and version-controlled in one place, so the wrong revision is not loaded from an operator's pen drive; production counts and tool life can be collected from every machine without walking the shop. Risk: the machines depend on the network and the server for new programs, so a server or network failure stops new jobs from starting, even though machines already running are unaffected.

quiz.q: Cutter radius compensation is easy on a CNC and almost impossible on hard-wired NC. Why?
quiz.a: Compensation needs the controller to offset every programmed point by the current tool radius, along the local path direction, and to handle inside corners and lead-in moves. That is arithmetic on stored blocks. Hard-wired logic has no stored program to recompute and no memory to hold the tool table.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern shops rarely buy a 'DNC system' as a product; they buy a network of CNCs and connect them with a machine-monitoring protocol such as MTConnect or OPC UA, which carries status and counters rather than just files. STEP-NC (ISO 14649) goes further and tries to send feature-level machining data instead of G code, so the controller chooses the cuts. Cloud dashboards now do the tool-life and utilisation tracking that distributed DNC started. Search for 'MTConnect', 'OPC UA machine tool' and 'STEP-NC' if you want to read ahead.
